1. Problem and dataset

Problem. Insurance fraud, such as staged accidents, claims for damage that happened before the policy started, or inflated repair bills, is a large hidden cost for insurers and their honest customers. Investigators cannot examine every claim, so they need a way to decide which claims to look at first. ClaimGuard is a binary classifier that estimates the probability that a vehicle-insurance claim is fraudulent, plus a web service that shows that score with concrete checks for the investigator. It is a triage tool: the model ranks, and a human decides.

Dataset. We use the public Vehicle Insurance Claim Fraud Detection dataset (fraud_oracle.csv, Oracle sample data, published on Kaggle by Shivam Bansal). It has 15,420 claims × 33 columns describing the policy holder (age, sex, marital status, driver rating, past claims, address change), the policy (base policy, deductible, agent type, days from policy start to accident), the vehicle (make, category, price band, age) and the accident (fault, area, police report, witness, dates). The label FraudFound_P is 1 for 923 claims (6.0%).

Data cleaning

  • Hidden missing values: Age = 0 in 320 rows (all in the youngest age band) is impossible. We set it to missing, then impute it with the training median plus an indicator flag.
  • One row with no claim date (DayOfWeekClaimed = '0') was dropped. The copy we downloaded also had 3 extra columns that are not in the original data; we dropped them.
  • Category cleaning: misspelt makes (Accura, Nisson, Mecedes, Porche) were corrected, and makes with fewer than 0.5% of rows were grouped as "Other".
  • Feature engineering: claim_delay_weeks, the weeks between accident and claim, was built from six calendar columns.
  • Feature selection: we removed ID-like columns (PolicyNumber, RepNumber), redundant ones (PolicyType = vehicle category + base policy; AgeOfPolicyHolder = banded Age), a near-constant one (Days_Policy_Claim, 99.5% one value) and Year, which cannot generalise to future claims. That leaves 21 input features: 4 numeric, 6 binary, 7 ordinal and 4 nominal.

EDA highlights

Figure 1. Class balance: 6% fraud.
Figure 2. Age by class; fraud rate by claim delay.
Figure 3. Fraud rate by fault, base policy and days from policy start to accident (dashed line: overall 6%).
  • Severe imbalance (6%): accuracy is misleading, since "always genuine" scores 94%. We evaluate with ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, recall and F1, use class weights, and tune the decision threshold.
  • Fault and policy type dominate: fraud is about 8% when the holder is at fault but about 1% for third-party fault. On liability-only policies, which never pay for the holder's own car, fraud almost disappears (0.7%).
  • Timing: claims for accidents within days of a policy starting, and claims reported a week or more late, are riskier. A recent address change is also a red flag.

2. Data contract and preprocessing

The data contract is defined once in features.py and enforced by the Pydantic schema in app.py. For example, age is an int in 16–80, driver_rating 1–4, deductible 300–700 and claim_delay_weeks 0–52. Categorical fields accept only the listed values, typed as Literal[...]. Integers are strict, so "45", 45.5, null and NaN are rejected, as are missing and unknown extra fields. Every violation returns HTTP 422. The full table is in the README.

Preprocessing is a scikit-learn ColumnTransformer inside the model Pipeline, so it is fitted only on training data, and the identical steps run in the API:

StepColumnsTechniqueReason
Missing valuesageMedian imputation + missing-indicatorRobust to skew; the flag keeps the "unknown" signal
Binary encodingsex, fault, accident_area, police_report_filed, witness_present, agent_type0/1 with a fixed orderTwo values need only one column
Ordinal encodingvehicle_price, age_of_vehicle, past_number_of_claims, number_of_supplements, address_change_claim, number_of_cars, days_policy_accidentIntegers in an explicitly stated orderThe ranges have a natural order
One-hot encodingmarital_status, base_policy, vehicle_category, makeOneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")No order between categories
Scalingnumeric + ordinal (logistic regression only)StandardScalerGradient descent with an L2 penalty needs comparable scales; trees do not
Outliersage, claim_delay_weeks, deductibleIQR check, all keptValues are genuine (older drivers, late reports, real deductible options)
BinningageTested, not usedCV ROC-AUC was 0.8125 continuous vs 0.8117 binned; trees learn their own cut points

4. Experiments and model comparison

train.py takes the algorithm and hyperparameters as command-line arguments. It uses a stratified 80/20 split with a fixed seed. For each run, the decision threshold is tuned for maximum F1 on a validation slice (25%) of the training data. The model is then refitted on the full training set and scored once on the test set. We ran 7 configurations of 3 algorithms:

RunAlgorithmHyperparametersROC-AUCPR-AUCRecallPrecisionF1
1Logistic RegressionC=1.00.8040.1510.4860.1630.244
2Logistic RegressionC=0.050.8040.1500.5300.1570.242
3Random Forestn_estimators=100, max_depth=60.8230.2050.7510.1540.255
4Random Forestn_estimators=300, max_depth=12, leaf=30.8200.1970.5620.1600.249
5Random Forestn_estimators=500, leaf=50.8180.2010.6110.1560.248
6HistGradientBoostinglr=0.1, iter=200, depth=40.8330.2410.3350.2180.264
7HistGradientBoostinglr=0.05, iter=400, depth=60.8330.2460.8320.1450.247
Figure 5. MLflow UI showing the 7 tracked runs.
Figure 6. Test ROC curves (notebook models).
Figure 7. Permutation importance of the chosen model.

Model choice: HistGradientBoosting (run 7)

  • Best PR-AUC (0.246), about 4× the 0.06 a random ranking would get, and the best ROC-AUC (0.833). For a rare positive class, PR-AUC is the most honest summary of ranking quality.
  • Highest recall (83%) at the tuned threshold (0.58). In triage, a missed fraud costs far more than sending an extra genuine claim to an investigator. Run 6 has a slightly higher F1 but catches only 34% of frauds.
  • It captures interactions such as "holder at fault and policy covers own car", which logistic regression cannot represent without hand-made features. Random forest came second.
  • Small and fast: about 1 MB on disk, with millisecond predictions.

The confusion matrix (test set, tuned threshold) is in the notebook. Precision is about 15%: roughly one flagged claim in seven is fraud, against one in seventeen at random. For an investigation queue this is a useful 2.4× lift, but it confirms the model should not reject claims automatically.

5. Testing, CI and deployment

Automated tests (18, all passing)

  • Health: /health returns 200 and model_loaded: true. UI: / serves the HTML page.
  • Domain logic: a claim with red flags (accident in the first week of an all-perils policy, address changed under 6 months ago, holder at fault, no police report or witness, reported 6 weeks late) must score higher than a routine third-party, liability-only claim. Changing only fault to "Policy Holder" must raise the risk.
  • Boundary (422): age 15 and 81, driver rating 5, negative delay, deductible 1000, "45", 45.5, null, unknown fault, unknown price band, unknown make, missing field, extra field.
  • Tips: every response carries 2–3 rule-based tips. Logging: each prediction adds one line to the log.
Figure 8. pytest -v output.

Continuous integration

.github/workflows/ci.yml runs on every push to main. Job 1 sets up Python 3.11, installs requirements.txt, trains a baseline random forest (--n_estimators 100 --max_depth 6) into a throwaway MLflow database, and runs pytest -v. Job 2 builds the Docker image, starts it, checks /health and /, asserts that invalid input returns 422, and prints the image size. [Insert screenshot of the green check.]

Docker

The image uses python:3.11-slim and installs only requirements-serve.txt (FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, joblib). MLflow, pytest, matplotlib and Jupyter stay out, so the image is smaller, builds faster and has less attack surface. That is the reason for having two requirements files. Size: about 695 MB on disk (about 140 MB compressed). It runs as a non-root user, has a HEALTHCHECK, and honours $PORT.

Deployment and monitoring

The container is deployed on Render's free tier from the GitHub repository, with automatic restarts. Every /predict request is logged as JSON (timestamp, input, probability, label) to logs/predictions.jsonl; a sample is in docs/sample_predictions.jsonl. drift_check.py (bonus) compares the logged inputs with the training data. It flags a numeric feature whose mean moves more than 0.5 training standard deviations, or a category whose share moves more than 15 percentage points, and exits with code 1 so it can trigger retraining.

6. Limitations and next steps

  • Old, narrow data: US claims from 1994–1996. Prices, cars and fraud tactics have changed, so the model needs retraining on current, local data before real use.
  • Few positives and coarse inputs: only 923 frauds, and many fields are pre-bucketed ranges. This caps precision at about 15%. More data, exact values (amounts, dates, repair-shop IDs) and network features (shared phone numbers or garages) would help most.
  • Fairness: sex and marital_status are protected attributes. A production system should test for disparate impact and probably drop them.
  • Monitoring: the drift check is manual today. Next steps: run it on a schedule, add continuous deployment after CI passes, add SHAP explanations per prediction, and record investigators' outcomes as fresh labels for retraining.
